extracted.subtask_description: Advice and stylistic rules for composing short humorous or satirical periodical essays (Spectator-style), including use of personae, innuendo, punctuation/omission devices, and tactics to attract readers without overt offence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit self-reference in non-persona pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: In Works of Humour, especially when a Man writes under a fictitious Personage, the talking of one's self may give some Diversion to the Publick; but I would advise every other Writer never to speak of himself, unless there be something very considerable in his Character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person or autobiographical remarks principally when writing under a fictional persona or when the author's character is notably interesting; otherwise avoid speaking of yourself to prevent vanity or irrelevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passing off repeated jests as original
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of egotists who repeat as Sayings of their own several Jests which were made before they were born — they ought to read jest-collections to see that their 'new' conceits have appeared in print already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check common jest-books and prior publications (example: Oxford and Cambridge Jests) before claiming witticisms as original; failing to do so marks a writer as vain or shallow and undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fictitious correspondents/personae for comic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing under a fictitious Personage may give some Diversion to the Publick; letters from imaginary characters (e.g., 'Blank') provide material for humour and satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt imaginary correspondents or personae to enable playful exaggeration, social observation, or comic complaint that would be awkward or offensive if stated directly by the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ blanks, dashes, and asterisks to create mystery and saleability
rubrics_metrics.description: A sprinkling of dashes, initials, or blanks (M and h, T and r, asterisks) that imply famous names makes a work more taking; readers enjoy deciphering and this practice helps sell insipid pamphlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partial redaction (initials, dashes, blanks, asterisks) to suggest well-known persons without explicit naming — this invites reader participation, increases curiosity, and helps market the piece. Examples given: 'M' and 'h', use of *** and &c--'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use provocative/charged terms (italicized) to attract attention
rubrics_metrics.description: A sprinkling of the Words 'Faction, Frenchman, Papist, Plunderer,' and the like significant Terms, in an Italick Character, have also a very good Effect upon the Eye of the Purchaser.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a few bold or charged words—preferably emphasized typographically—to catch the reader's eye and stimulate interest, but balance this with caution about offence (see innuendo guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ innuendo and oblique phrasing to satirize without direct libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Party-writers are sensible of the secret Virtue of an Innuendo; they omit vowels or use dashes so as to hint at persons or charges without direct naming; 'two Dashes into his Pudding' is used as a way to be cautious of giving offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor indirect insinuation (innuendo, parenthetical hints, redactions) to make pointed criticism while avoiding legal or moral consequences of direct accusation. This allows you to attack character or policy subtly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use syncopation (vowel-omission) and other obfuscations as satirical device
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors omit only the Vowels of a great Man's Name, and fall most unmercifully upon all the Consonants; this way of Writing was introduced by T-m Br-wn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately remove vowels or otherwise garble names to lampoon public figures while preserving plausible deniability and adding comic effect; this is a recognized satirical technique (called 'syncopists' here).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage readers with enigmas and puzzles in the text
rubrics_metrics.description: I have drawn up a very curious Libel ... I shall leave this with my curious Reader, as some ingenious Writers do their Enigmas, and if any sagacious Person can fairly unriddle it, I will print his Explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed puzzles, concealed meanings, or 'libels' that invite readers to decode them; publishing the solution later rewards engaged readers and foments discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage scandal or illustrious names to sell copy (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Few Writings sell which are not filled with great Names and illustrious Titles. The Reader generally casts his Eye upon a new Book, and if he finds several Letters separated from one another by a Dash, he buys it up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention or insinuate famous people, scandals, or factional controversies to increase reader interest and sales, but temper such strategies with indirectness and typographical obfuscation to avoid libel or undue offence.
